entries.1.202: He surveyed the ocean, its shores, the trees born upon those shores, and the mouths of the ocean's wives as well.
entries.1.203: Considering himself, wise and self-possessed, to resemble a great cloud and as though to block the sky, he formed a resolve.
entries.1.204: "As soon as the rakshasas see the swelling of my body and my speed," thought that great-minded one, "they will grow curious about me."
entries.1.205: Then, drawing in that body which resembled a mountain, he resumed his natural form, as a self-possessed man who has been freed of delusion.

entries.1.207: Wearing many fair forms at will and unassailable by his foes, having taken form, surveyed himself and weighed his purpose, he reached the further shore of the sea.

entries.1.209: Then, having reached the sea-shore and beheld Lanka upon the crest of that best of mountains, the monkey shook off his form and alighted on that mountain, startling the beasts and birds.

entries.58.59: — pale as a lotus in winter, resolved upon death and averse to living —
entries.58.60: — such was she whom, guessing by these marks, I took to be Sita, wife of Rama.

entries.67.17: The crow, once released, regained its own abode. "Thus, though you are the best among knowers of missiles, of great being and of good character too —
entries.67.18: "— for what reason, Raghava, do you not employ the missile against the rakshasas? Neither danavas nor gandharvas, neither asuras nor the hosts of Maruts —
entries.67.19: "— are able so to contend with you in battle, Rama. If you the valorous have any concern for me —
entries.67.20: "— let Ravana be slain swiftly in battle with keen shafts; or let Lakshmana, scorcher of foes, receive his brother's command.
entries.67.21: "For what reason does that best of men, Raghava, not protect me? Those two tigers among men, of splendour equal to wind and fire, are able —
entries.67.22: "— and unassailable even to the gods: for what reason do they overlook me? Surely some great misdeed of mine alone is the cause —
entries.67.23: "— in that those two scorchers of foes, though able and together, do not protect me." Having heard the piteous and well-spoken word of Vaidehi,
entries.67.24: I spoke to her once again: "Lady, I swear to you by truth, Rama is turned away from all but grief for you.
entries.67.25: "And when Rama is overcome with sorrow, Lakshmana burns with it. Your ladyship has been found at last; this is no time for grieving.
entries.67.26: "In this very moment, radiant lady, you shall see the end of your sorrows. Those two tigers among men, princes and scorchers of foes,
entries.67.27: "their zeal roused by the sight of you, shall reduce Lanka to ashes; and having slain in battle the terrible Ravana with his kinsmen,
entries.67.28: "Raghava shall assuredly lead you to his own city, fair one. And what token, blameless one, Rama would recognise,
entries.67.29: "begetting joy in him, that you should give me." She looked round all the quarters, and from her garment
entries.67.30: "loosed the excellent knot of her braid and gave me this gem, O you of great strength. Receiving the gem in both hands for your sake, beloved of the Raghus,
entries.67.31: "I saluted her with my head and made haste to return. Seeing my zeal made ready for the going, the lady of fair complexion,
entries.67.32: "as I swelled in size, addressed me, the daughter of Janaka, her face full of tears, piteous, her speech choked with weeping.
entries.67.33: "Startled by my springing up and struck by the surge of grief, Sita then said to me: 'You are blessed, great monkey,
entries.67.34: "'in that you shall see the mighty-armed and lotus-eyed Rama, and the mighty-armed and illustrious Lakshmana, my brother-in-law.'
entries.67.35: "Addressed thus by Sita, I spoke to Maithili: 'Lady, delight of Janaka, mount swiftly upon my back,
entries.67.36: "'that today I may show you your lord Raghava, greatly blessed and dark-eyed one, with Sugriva and with Lakshmana.'
entries.67.37: "Then that lady said to me: 'Great monkey, bull among vanaras, that I should of my own will resort to your back — this is no dharma.
entries.67.38: "'And formerly, hero, I was touched upon the limbs by the rakshasa; what could I do therein, sore pressed by time?
entries.67.39: "'Go, tiger among monkeys, where those two sons of the king are.'" Having spoken thus, she set herself to send a further message.
entries.67.40: "'Hanuman, ask after the welfare of those two, Rama and Lakshmana, like two lions, and of Sugriva with his ministers, and of all.
entries.67.41: "'And how that mighty-armed Raghava shall carry me across this flood of sorrow that hems me in — that you should declare.
entries.67.42: "'Tell Rama, when you have come to his presence, of this fierce surge of grief of mine and of the threatening of these rakshasas; and may your road be auspicious, foremost hero of the vanaras.'"
entries.67.43: Self-restrained, that noble lady Sita spoke this word to you in sorrow, O king. Understanding it as it was uttered, believe Sita to be wholly in safety.
